top.line: Above the mechanics, an agent's policy is business logic
top.para: The first agent rules are mechanical and vendors handle them well, but a few layers up a behaviour policy describes how the company works and what it is for. Much of that was never written down because software was the law, so it must now be written in layers, each with its own owner.

s0.line: Mechanical controls are vendors' strength and need measuring
s0.para: The bottom layers are mechanical: the agent's own account, a platform-held token, delete switched off, outside forwarding blocked, sending needing a person. These are real boundaries. When the Google Workspace agent measured its connector on 19 September it found thirty tools, with send_message running unprompted while trashing needed approval.

s1.line: One layer up, the rules become the firm's business
s1.para: Above the mechanics sit function, process, relationship and organisation: reply in threads, never quote a price, invoice only after finance approval, nothing to a client in dispute except through legal, treat customers fairly. Each is a sentence a manager would say, and each layer has a different owner.

s2.line: Vendors build what is the same for every customer
s2.para: A control platform must scale, so it builds roles, switches, secret stores and approval prompts. The business layers differ per company, change weekly and are often unwritten. A vendor that models each customer becomes a consultancy, so the mechanical layer is a product and the business layers are the customer's to write.

s3.line: Software enforced the rules nobody wrote down
s3.para: Companies never wrote their business logic down because their software was the law: no button to send an unapproved invoice, no screen showing payment details. An agent calls the API the button would have called, so a rule the interface enforced by omission is lost unless written in the behaviour policy and enforced.

s4.line: Behaviour policies nest inside each other, layer by layer
s4.para: The structure that holds this is fractal: foundational controls, then soft controls, then function, process and relationship, with the company's purpose at the top. A policy describes rather than judges. It uses the same grammar as the site's fractal semantic graphs and the ABP's three-layer vocabulary.

s5.line: Of seventeen rules, five are controls and six hope
s5.para: Each rule is backed by a control, governed by an accepted risk, or resting on hope. In the example five of seventeen are controls, six accepted risks and six hope. The platform layer is all control, the organisation layer all hope, and the more firm-specific a rule, the more it rests on behaviour.

s6.line: Vendors plug in by enforcing a written rule
s6.para: A vendor need only enforce the rules its product can reach: a send gateway, an outbound content check, a finance approval lookup, a legal blocked-recipients list each move a rule towards control. A control tied to a written rule shows what was bought, matching what RG.2 and AC.3 of the AI Baseline Control Framework ask.

s7.line: The upper layers read like a skill with controls
s7.para: A skill says how a function is done; a policy layer says what is allowed, who owns the rule and what stands in the way. Written together they codify the business for an agent, letting knowledge from a few heads and unreadable software be followed, reviewed and enforced, so the business can scale.

s8.line: Next, a real inbox counted before and after
s8.para: The fictional example comes next as a real one: the measured Gmail deployment as the bottom layers, upper layers written for one real inbox, the three states counted and published as a vault, then repeated with a vendor's control. Drafted from Dinis Cruz's voice note on 7 October 2026; no vendor was contacted.
